clue.text: I tore a male to pieces to effect an improvement

indicators.note: tearing something to pieces breaks it up, so these letters are scattered and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A violent scene in which a man is torn apart, oddly described as making things better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pieces' rearranges the ten letters of I TORE A MALE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ameliorate is to make better, which is bringing about an improvement.

clue.text: Cite a fourth-rate Italian leader

parts.note: D is the fourth grade after A, B and C
Il Duce was the title of Mussolini, Italy's fascist leader

explanation.surface: Naming an Italian politician who is far from top class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian leader' tempts you to take the first letter I; it is DUCE, Mussolini's title.
explanation.definitionFit: To adduce is to bring forward as evidence, quoting it in support of an argument.

clue.text: Consuming passion for pigs

explanation.surface: A greedy obsession attributed to pigs.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking in food is consuming it, and pigs are proverbially devoted to their food.

clue.text: Periphrastic discourse reported by others

explanation.surface: A grammar note about roundabout talk passed on second-hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Reported speech is roundabout, not quoting words directly, and it is what is relayed by someone else.

clue.text: Transported wild orchids without additional premium

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps round another
wild suggests something growing out of order, so the letters of orchids are rearranged

parts.note: AP is the insurance abbreviation for additional premium

explanation.surface: Exotic orchids shipped over with no extra insurance charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking: the anagram of ORCHIDS, RHSODIC, goes round AP.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhapsodic means ecstatic, carried away with delight.

clue.text: American sweetheart blows the whistle

explanation.surface: An American darling who acts as a referee.
explanation.definitionFit: Toots is a US term of endearment like honey, and it also means sounds a horn or whistle.

clue.text: Yearn for a clear-headed man

indicators.note: clear-headed is read as the head of the word clear, its opening letter only

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: Longing for a man who thinks straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clear-headed' looks like one adjective; split it so 'headed' takes only C from 'clear'.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache for something is to long for it badly, an idiom for yearning.

clue.text: About to set up some friend? Rubbish!

parts.note: C stands for circa, about

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means lifted, read from bottom to top

parts.note: part means some of something
pal is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone about to introduce a friend, dismissed as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns PART + PAL into LAPTRAP, which follows C.
explanation.definitionFit: Claptrap is empty, pretentious talk, nonsense.

clue.text: Adore old novel featuring a fabulous city

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are given a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Loving an old novel about a legendary city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: El Dorado was the mythical South American city of gold sought by explorers.

clue.text: Sweeping statement from Army chief ordered to Sinai

parts.note: a general is a senior army commander

indicators.note: ordered means put in order, so the letters of to Sinai are rearranged

explanation.surface: A senior officer receives orders to go to Sinai.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' reads as a command; it rearranges TO SINAI into ISATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A generalisation is a broad claim made without allowing for exceptions.

clue.text: Adored urging others to make hay

parts.note: 'Do!' is an exhortation telling others to act
to ted is to spread out mown grass to dry, an old farming word

explanation.surface: Someone adored for encouraging people to get on with haymaking.
explanation.walkthrough: TED is a dialect farming verb: to turn and spread grass so it dries into hay; 'Do ted!' is the urging.
explanation.definitionFit: Doted means loved to excess, so it is the past tense of adoring someone foolishly.

clue.text: Previously stated that a warning of course was given

parts.note: fore is the cry a golfer gives on the course to warn others of a ball in flight
said, as in a statement that was uttered or delivered

explanation.surface: A formal report that a warning had already been issued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but it is the golf course: FORE! is the golfer's warning shout.
explanation.definitionFit: Aforesaid is the legal word for something mentioned earlier in the same document.

clue.text: Key institutions about to invest in US currency

indicators.note: to invest is to put money into something, and here one word is placed inside another

parts.note: cents are units of American money
re is the Latin-derived word for about or concerning

explanation.surface: A financial tip about putting money into American dollars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invest in' suggests finance, but it puts RE inside CENTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Centres are main hubs, the most important places where an activity is organised.

clue.text: Clothing for a Devonshire diner?

parts.note: a garment that sounds like someone who eats the sweet cream teas Devon is famous for

explanation.surface: A question about what to wear when eating in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: Devonshire is an English county famous for cream teas; a jumper's name is punned as a 'sweet eater' who enjoys them.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted jumper is a garment, and its name sounds like a lover of sweet things.

clue.text: Scottish school gains a minor film prize

parts.note: in Scotland many secondary schools are called academies
a ward is a child under a guardian, a minor in law

explanation.surface: A school in Scotland wins a small award for a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minor' looks like an adjective for the prize, but it is a noun: a WARD is a minor in legal care.
explanation.definitionFit: An Academy Award, or Oscar, is the best-known prize in the film industry.

clue.text: Girl gets a farewell greeting in London

parts.note: maid is a literary word for a girl
vale is Latin for farewell

explanation.surface: A girl gets a goodbye.
explanation.walkthrough: MAIDA VALE is a district of north-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Maida Vale is a residential district in the capital, so it is somewhere located there.

clue.text: In working order for successful surgery

explanation.surface: A patient fit for an operation.
explanation.definitionFit: Operable means able to function, and also able to be treated by an operation.

clue.text: Small problem for a punctilious man

parts.note: a tickler is a tricky puzzle or problem

explanation.surface: A minor difficulty for a fussy man.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler insists on exact correctness, a pedant about detail.

clue.text: How to make a large shoe fit? Give over!

definitions.text: How to make a large shoe fit?

explanation.surface: Advice for fitting outsized footwear, then an exasperated plea to stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuffing hosiery inside a roomy shoe makes it fit, and the same phrase is British slang telling someone to shut up.

clue.text: Get punished for taking a glass of sherry

parts.note: to cop it is British slang for getting into trouble

explanation.surface: Being punished for drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: COP IT is British slang for being punished.
explanation.definitionFit: A copita is the tulip-shaped glass used for sherry in Spain.

clue.text: He heard it, but he not." (Byron)

definitions.text: He heard it, but he not." (Byron)

parts.words: He heard it, but he not." (Byron)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Childe Harold, where the dying gladiator ignores the crowd's roar

explanation.surface: A line of Byron's poetry with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line from Byron's Childe Harold reads with the missing word between 'he' and 'not'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing past-tense verb means paid attention to, completing Byron's line.

clue.text: One church amidst others is most affluent

indicators.note: amidst means in the middle of, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: the rest means the others
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A single church among many is the wealthiest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amidst' puts I and CH inside REST.
explanation.definitionFit: The richest is the one with the most money, the wealthiest.

clue.text: Head-dress I found in the seat of Irish kings

indicators.note: found in signals that one letter is placed inside the place name

parts.note: the Hill of Tara in County Meath was the seat of the High Kings of Ireland

explanation.surface: A crown discovered at the ancient Irish royal site.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled ornamental crown worn on the head.

clue.text: In Paris it's fashionable

parts.note: the French phrase meaning in the current style, borrowed into English

explanation.surface: A remark that something is in vogue in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' signals that the answer is French: the phrase means 'in the fashion'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means in the style of the moment, so it describes something stylish.

clue.text: Helmet needed to extract barium, resin and molten rock

parts.note: Ba is the chemical symbol for barium
lac is a resin secreted by insects, used in shellac
lava is molten rock from a volcano

explanation.surface: A mining or chemistry scene where a helmet protects against minerals and lava.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extract' suggests removing, but here it is just part of the link 'needed to extract'.
explanation.definitionFit: A balaclava is a knitted head covering, a soft hood named after the Crimean War battle.

clue.text: Epic one encountered 1944 years ago

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
counted back from the puzzle's publication in 1995 this is the year 51, written LI AD in Roman style

explanation.surface: A heroic tale someone came across from nearly two thousand years back.
explanation.walkthrough: The date is relative to when the puzzle appeared: 1995 minus 1944 is AD 51, Roman LI AD. 'encountered' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's poem of the Trojan War is the archetypal epic.

clue.text: Spanish banker in Hebron

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the place name Hebron

explanation.surface: A Spanish financier working in the West Bank city.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'banker' is a river, something with banks; Hebron is a city in the West Bank.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ebro is a major river of north-east Spain, and a river has banks.

clue.text: Control and cheat a labourer

parts.note: to take in is to deceive or swindle
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: Managing staff and swindling a worker.
explanation.definitionFit: To take something in hand is to assume charge of it, an idiom for controlling.
